title: Health economic impact and cost threshold for switching from bivalent to nonavalent HPV vaccination for preadolescent girls in KwaZulu Natal, South Africa: A mathematical modeling analysis accounting for the HIV epidemic
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, University of Washington, Stellenbosch University, Columbia University - Irving Medical Center, Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation, Harvard University - Massachusetts General Hospital and University of Washington

detail.title: Health economic impact and cost threshold for switching from bivalent to nonavalent HPV vaccination for preadolescent girls in KwaZulu Natal, South Africa: A mathematical modeling analysis accounting for the HIV epidemic
detail.abstract: Background: Human papillomavirus bivalent (2vHPV) and nonavalent (9vHPV) vaccines demonstrate effectiveness against HPV types causing 70% and 90% of cervical cancers, respectively. Current South African guidelines recommend vaccinating girls ages 9-14 with one dose of 2vHPV. Switching recommendations to 9vHPV has the potential to avert more cervical cancer burden, but the cost-effectiveness and cost-threshold at which 9vHPV would provide good value for money in South Africa is unknown.Methods: Using a validated compartmental HPV and HIV transmission model parameterized to KwaZulu-Natal, South Africa, we simulated scenarios of 2vHPV and 9vHPV implementation over 100 years with two doses (72% coverage) and one dose (80% and 90% coverage) and evaluated scenarios assuming lifelong or waning single-dose vaccine efficacy. We estimated cervical cancer cases and deaths averted for single-dose vaccination with 9vHPV vs. 2vHPV at 80% coverage. We estimated the health impacts and maximum cost/dose at which 9vHPV would be cost-effective using willingness-to-pay thresholds ranging from $500/DALY averted to $3,015/DALY averted (2023 USD). We also assessed the health impacts and incremental cost-effectiveness ratios (ICERs) of 9vHPV at current costs ($110/dose) compared to 2vHPV ($9.23/dose).Results:  Single-dose 9vHPV at 80% coverage could avert 7.9% more cervical cancer cases and 6.4% more deaths than 2vHPV (lifelong efficacy scenario). The maximum per-dose cost for 9vHPV to be cost-effective (lifelong efficacy and 80% coverage) ranged from $15 ($500/DALY averted threshold) to $45/dose ($3,015/DALY averted threshold). Assuming waning single-dose efficacy, maximum 9vHPV per dose costs ranged from $15 to $50/dose, depending on the threshold. At current market costs, single-dose 9vHPV at 90% coverage exceeds commonly used cost-effective thresholds with ICERs of $10,480/DALY averted (lifelong efficacy) and $8,806/DALY averted (waning efficacy).Conclusions: Implementing 9vHPV can result in greater reduction of cervical cancer burden than 2vHPV, but vaccine cost needs to be reduced for 9vHPV to be cost-effective in KwaZulu-Natal.

title: When Nudges Backfire: How Not To Improve Attitudes Towards Shared E-Scooters
affiliations: University of Warwick and University of Warwick

detail.title: When Nudges Backfire: How Not To Improve Attitudes Towards Shared E-Scooters
detail.abstract: As part of a push towards sustainable transportation, there have been several rental e-scooter trials in UK cities. However, vandalism and mistreatment have plagued these schemes, and the adoption of e-scooters remains low. We test the effectiveness of nudges designed to improve attitudes and uptake of shared e-scooters. These nudges are based on three main mechanisms: ownership, social norm messaging, and social status signalling. We find that our main ownership and social status nudges are not only ineffective, they worsen attitudes towards shared e-scooters and reduce intended uptake. Injunctive norm messaging did not have any significant impact on stated adoption or willingness to report misuse. Our results highlight the potential consequences of nudges that backfire. We recommend carefully testing proposed nudges within the intended context before implementation, even if they have been successful in a different context, in order to avoid negative consequences.

title: Tax Avoidance and ESG Disclosure Mandate: International Evidence
affiliations: University of Alberta - Campus Saint-Jean, University of South Carolina - Moore School of Business, Santa Clara University - Leavey School of Business and University of Texas at El Paso

detail.title: Tax Avoidance and ESG Disclosure Mandate: International Evidence
detail.abstract:
This paper examines how regulations mandating environmental, social, and governance (ESG) disclosure affect an important dimension of a firm’s financial decision, namely its tax payments. Using a difference-in-differences analysis on a sample of firms from 48 countries, we find that ESG disclosure mandates lead to significant reductions in tax 
avoidance, with stronger effects for mandates that include tax-relevant components. We identify increases in ESG information transparency and improvements in firms’ ESG 
performance as channels through which ESG disclosure mandates reduce tax avoidance. We further find that the decrease in tax avoidance following ESG disclosure mandates is more pronounced in countries with weaker financial disclosure requirements, weaker legal and tax enforcement, and weaker environmental and social institutions. Collectively, the evidence suggests that non-financial disclosure regulations can curb aggressive tax behavior, supporting broader goals of corporate accountability and sustainable development.

title: Work From Home and the Post-COVID Spending Surge
affiliations: University of Virginia - Darden School of Business

detail.title: Work From Home and the Post-COVID Spending Surge
detail.abstract: U.S. personal saving rates have remained below pre-pandemic levels. This paper links the sustained increase in consumption to the rise of working from home (WFH). Using PSID 2019-2023 data and an industry-based instrument for WFH, I find that households induced to WFH raised expenditure by more than $7,000 on average, holding income and wealth constant. Spending rose not only among movers but also among non-movers, consistent with a persistent shift in preferences toward housing-complementary consumption. The estimates imply that WFH reduced the aggregate saving rate by 1.2 percentage points, and they suggest that remote work structurally increased demand for housing-related consumption, contributing to the post-pandemic spending boom.

title: Intelligent Waste Collection Optimization Using AI And IoT in urban Environments
affiliations: University of Toronto - Department of Civil Engineering, McGill University - School of Computer Science, University of Toronto - Department of Civil Engineering, McGill University - School of Computer Science and University of Toronto - Department of Civil Engineering

detail.title: Intelligent Waste Collection Optimization Using AI And IoT in urban Environments
detail.abstract: Efficient waste collection remains a critical challenge in rapidly urbanizing cities, where conventional fixed-route systems often result in redundant trips and overflow incidents. This study proposes an integrated framework that combines IoT-based fill-level sensing, short-term prediction using long short-term memory (LSTM) networks, and route optimization through a capacity-constrained traveling salesman problem (TSP) model solved by genetic algorithms. A three-month pilot was conducted across 150 collection points in a high-density district, with two experimental groups using the AI-IoT framework and one control group operating under conventional schedules. The results demonstrated that the experimental districts achieved a 24.8% reduction in redundant collection trips and a 30.2% decrease in overflow incidents, both statistically significant at p < 0.05. Furthermore, the LSTM prediction module reached a coefficient of determination of R² = 0.92 with a mean absolute error of 0.07, outperforming baseline regression methods. These findings confirm that integrating predictive analytics and IoT-enabled monitoring within a closed feedback loop can deliver measurable environmental and operational benefits. The framework not only enhances immediate efficiency but also provides a scalable model for sustainable urban waste management.

title: Preferences for Individual Metering and Billing

detail.title: Preferences for Individual Metering and Billing

declarations.funderStatement: The research was supported by the Swiss National Science Foundation (Project 201958).

detail.abstract: Millions of households around the world must share utility bills with their neighbors due to a lack of household-specific meters. Individual metering and billing has been shown to strongly reduce consumption of heat, electricity, and water, but households' willingness to pay the costs of metering is unknown. This study uses a survey experiment augmented with administrative data to study preferences in buildings with and without individual metering and billing. We find overwhelming support for individual metering and billing, even with relatively high costs, and even among high consumers who stand to pay less with common billing.

title: The Future of Green and Blue Hydrogen in the Energy Transition and Net Zero Agenda
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: The Future of Green and Blue Hydrogen in the Energy Transition and Net Zero Agenda
detail.abstract:
As the global energy system undergoes a historic transformation toward decarbonisation, hydrogen has emerged as a cornerstone of future clean energy strategies. Increasingly recognised for its potential to decarbonise hard-to-abate sectors—such as heavy industry, long-distance transport, chemicals, and high-temperature manufacturing—hydrogen is being positioned by governments and industries as a key enabler of net-zero pathways. Among its various forms, green hydrogen, produced through electrolysis powered by renewable electricity, and blue hydrogen, generated from natural gas with carbon capture and storage (CCS), have gained the most traction in global policy and investment landscapes.

This paper critically evaluates the future of green and blue hydrogen in the context of the global energy transition, focusing on their respective contributions, limitations, and strategic roles in meeting mid-century net-zero targets. It explores key dimensions such as lifecycle greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions, production scalability, cost trajectories, infrastructure compatibility, and the evolving regulatory frameworks across major economies.

Green hydrogen, while currently more expensive, is projected to become cost-competitive by 2030 in regions with abundant renewable resources. Its alignment with zero-emission goals and declining technology costs suggest it will form the long-term foundation of a decarbonised hydrogen economy. However, its growth is dependent on the rapid expansion of renewable energy capacity, electrolyser innovation, water availability, and supportive grid infrastructure. Conversely, blue hydrogen offers a more immediately scalable pathway by leveraging existing natural gas and CCS infrastructure. It is particularly attractive to fossil fuel-producing nations seeking to remain relevant in a carbon-constrained world. Yet, blue hydrogen’s future is constrained by methane leakage risks, incomplete carbon capture, and increasing scrutiny of its lifecycle emissions.

The paper further investigates the regional policy preferences—from the European Union’s strong green hydrogen mandate, to the United States’ neutral but incentive-rich Inflation Reduction Act (IRA), to hybrid strategies in the Middle East and Asia. It also examines the emergence of international hydrogen trade corridors, certification regimes, and the implications for global energy geopolitics.

Environmental and social trade-offs are addressed, including water use in electrolysis, CCS permanence concerns, and the need for a just and equitable hydrogen transition in developing economies. The analysis concludes that while green and blue hydrogen will coexist in the near term, the net-zero future will be predominantly green. Strategic deployment, targeted public policy, and emissions transparency will be essential to ensuring that hydrogen delivers meaningful climate benefits rather than serving as a low-ambition alternative.

Ultimately, this paper argues that hydrogen is not a silver bullet, but rather a critical piece of the decarbonisation puzzle that must be integrated into broader system-wide changes—including renewable electrification, energy efficiency, carbon pricing, and international cooperation. Decisions made in the next decade regarding hydrogen pathways will significantly influence whether the world can meet its climate commitments and ensure a sustainable, equitable energy future.

detail.abstract: In the context of the ICDS 2025 (2nd International Conference on Digital Sovereignty; Track 5 Geopolitics and Trust), this paper examines how data sovereignties have become a foundational challenge in the GenAI era. The monopolistic power of Big Tech platforms—so-called data-opolies—undermines democratic accountability, reshapes political agency, and destabilizes institutional trust by concentrating data flows within opaque algorithmic infrastructures and extractive AI economies. The paper reframes data sovereignty as an issue that manifests directly in technical domains, ranging from cybersecurity protocols and interoperable cloud architectures to federated learning systems and algorithmic accountability frameworks. Rather than treating sovereignty as an abstract principle, the analysis shows how it must be embedded in infrastructures, protocols, and governance models that balance social values with computational design. Yet, the computer science community has only marginally engaged with these debates, focusing on narrow technical fixes without addressing the structural asymmetries of data power. This paper issues a wake-up call: sovereignty is a systems-level design problem that demands interdisciplinary engagement. Against the extractive logic driving GenAI economics, the paper highlights emancipatory alternatives such as data cooperatives, public-interest digital commons, and accountability mechanisms rooted in civic participation. These models introduce new requirements for scalability, privacy, and incentive design that cannot be resolved without computer science contributions. Empirical illustrations from electoral infrastructures and urban data governance highlight vulnerabilities to asymmetry and opportunities for sovereignty-building. The paper advances a roadmap for policymakers, civil society, and technologists to embed sovereignty in trustworthy, resilient, and geopolitically relevant digital infrastructures.

title: Debt Accumulation and Default in Low-Income Countries
affiliations: Loyola University Maryland - Department of Economics and Federal Housing Finance Agency

detail.title: Debt Accumulation and Default in Low-Income Countries
detail.abstract: This paper studies the accumulation of external public debt in low-income countries (LICs) after receiving debt relief from multilateral lenders. While LICs who received debt relief from the International Monetary Fund in the early 2000s generally lowered their external debt in the initial years of relief, many experienced fast resurgence in debt after borrowing limits were lifted in 2006. Using a difference-in-differences model, we find countries that benefited from the relaxation are more likely to experience a significant increase in their debt-to-GDP ratio. We quantitatively evaluate the effects of debt limit relaxation using a model of sovereign default with two types of debt: subsidized loans from multilateral institutions and non-concessional loans from the private market. The model is calibrated using data from Mozambique prior to its default in 2016, and we find that an impatient government is necessary to match the data on debt accumulation and investment. In the calibrated model, lifting limits on non-concessional borrowing results in a 17.1 percent loss in households' consumption-equivalent welfare. Furthermore, the welfare benefits of relaxing borrowing limits with a counter-factually patient government are relatively small.

title: Meaningful Change Index: A P-Value Independent Metric for Assessing Robustness and Fragility in Continuous Outcomes
affiliations: University of Washington - School of Medicine

detail.title: Meaningful Change Index: A P-Value Independent Metric for Assessing Robustness and Fragility in Continuous Outcomes

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing interests.

detail.abstract:
The assessment of statistical robustness in clinical trials with continuous outcomes has relied heavily on p-value dependent metrics that fail to address clinically meaningful differences. This study introduces the Meaningful Change Index - MeCI - a novel metric applied to continuous data that quantifies how distinguishable treatment groups are based on the crossover point of their sample distributions. It is independent of statistical significance testing. The Meaningful Change Index is defined as the minimum distance from group means to their distributional crossover point, normalized by the combined standard deviations. Unlike existing continuous fragility indices that depend on p-value thresholds, Meaningful Change Index focuses on a statistically meaningful numeric separation between populations. A worked example demonstrates temporal patterns of treatment effect evolution, revealing how group distinguishability changes over time despite robust binary outcomes when arbitrary thresholds are applied to the data. Meaningful Change Index provides clinically relevant fragility and robustness assessment for continuous data without dependence on statistical significance conventions, offering superior insights into treatment effect sustainability and group separation.

Version 2: Terminology updated from 'Meaningful Change Fragility (MCF)' to 'Meaningful Change Index (MeCI)' (MEK-see-eye) for clarity and collision avoidance. Core methodology unchanged.

detail.abstract: Today, in the fast and competitive business environment, fashion entrepreneurs must adapt to the ever-evolving fashion trends to withstand the market. Customer satisfaction and the tastes of younger generations, particularly Gen Z, greatly influence the fashion industry. With Gen Z's strong obligation to sustainability, there has been a significant shift toward fashion choices that align with ethical and cultural values. This study explores the connection of sustainable cultural trends and digital influence, examining how social media platforms, particularly Instagram, make it possible to promote and adopt ethnic fashion. The purpose of this research is to provide light on the interconnected nature of fashion, culture, and technology by investigating the impact of online influencers on consumers' fashion decisions. Specifically, the study focuses on how Instagram influencers promote ethnic wear among Gen Z women, highlighting their impact on the popularization of sustainable and culturally strengthening fashion trends. This study describes the demographic profile of the respondents. This research uses a simple random sampling technique alongside a descriptive research design. Factor analysis shows the most influential factors are social media influence, heritage, attitude of the younger generation, purchasing power, Instagram influencers, social responsibility, personal style and individuality, and price and affordability, and peer and friends adopting ethnic wear, while structural equation modeling (SEM) reveals the impact. The results highlight the importance of ethical and inclusive fashion practices and shed light on the influence of Instagram personalities on cultural sustainability as well as the fashion business.

detail.abstract:
This short article offers a practical guide for using AI tools to improve the judgment and efficiency of lawyers, mediators, and arbitrators.  It cites ABA Ethics Opinion 512, which describes lawyers’ ethical duty of technological competence under the ABA Model Rules.

The article encourages practitioners to begin by selecting AI tools appropriate to their tasks such as general-purpose platforms or specialized tools listed in the article.  It explains how to write effective prompts, use follow-up questions to refine outputs, and apply professional judgment when reviewing results.  It includes a list of suggested follow-up prompts.

Getting useful results from AI tools requires similar skills used in legal and dispute resolution work – skills that people can improve with practice.  The article includes numerous examples of AI prompts that can be used throughout the life of a case, from preparation to post-session reflection.

It cautions that AI tools can produce inaccurate, misleading, or fabricated content, and urges users to exercise human oversight and to independently verify results.

detail.abstract: The issue of the consequences of the ideology of genocide as a determining factor in the development of Russian society for the dynamics of international legal processes has become particularly relevant against the backdrop of the full-scale invasion of Ukraine by the Russian Federation. This study is devoted to analyzing the ways in which Russia identifies itself in the international legal field in the context of the genocide of the Ukrainian people. The article examines the system of Russian measures aimed at the genocide of Ukrainians, which involve ideological pressure and censorship. The study reveals the existence of a consistent Russian policy toward the Ukrainian people that bears signs of genocidal intent. The study argues that the propaganda of genocide within the Russian Federation's political narrative is suggestive in nature, and the strategy itself is a tool for Russia's self-identification in the international environment, which influences the dynamics of the international legal system. The article analyzes approaches to the definition of genocide and the peculiarities of the representation of this concept in legal documents relating to the protection of fundamental human rights. The main evolutionary stages of the genocide of the Ukrainian people and the ways in which Russia identifies itself on this basis are identified. The article analyzes the variability of forms of practical expression of genocide aimed at the loss of national identity: mass torture and killings, forced deportations, and sexual violence. Particular attention is paid to the expression of Russian ideology of genocide against Ukrainians in the context of modern military operations: massive shelling and missile strikes, destruction of infrastructure, moral and informational influence, psychological means of destruction. The vectors of influence of the Russian Federation's methods of self-identification on the dynamics of the system of international legal relations are characterized. The functionality of the international judicial system in the process of bringing war criminals to justice is investigated. The destructive critical consequences of the Russian Federation's genocidal ideology for the security of global geopolitical development are substantiated.

detail.title: DoW Effect in the Indian Stock Market: Evidence from NSE-200 and BSE-30 with Event-Study Analysis
detail.abstract: This study investigates the Day-of-the-Week effect in the Indian stock market using daily returns and trading volumes of the BSE-30 and NSE-200 indices over the period 2010-2025. The analysis addresses four objectives: (i) to test for the presence of weekday effects in stock returns, (ii) to examine weekday variations in trading volumes, (iii) to evaluate whether these anomalies weakened, strengthened, or disappeared following major structural and regulatory changes-including the 2014 government change, the 2016 demonetisation, and the 2020 COVID-19 pandemic, and (iv) to compare results between the BSE-30 and NSE-200 and provide recommendations for investors. Using pooled OLS regressions with weekday dummy variables (Friday as the benchmark), followed by panel Fixed Effects and Random Effects estimations, the results confirm the persistence of weekday anomalies in both indices. Returns analysis reveals a negative Monday effect across both indices and a positive Wednesday effect in the NSE-200. Trading volume analysis shows significantly lower activity on Mondays and higher activity mid-to end-week, with stronger and more diverse patterns in the NSE-200. Structural event analysis demonstrates that while the BSE-30 remained stable, anomalies in the NSE-200 were restructured, with Mondays turning negative and midweek returns turning strongly positive post-event. The findings suggest that the BSE-30 exhibits greater efficiency and resilience, making it more suitable for long-term investors, while the NSE-200 offers exploitable anomalies for active traders, though with higher risk. The persistence of anomalies, particularly in the broader market, underscores the need for regulatory measures to enhance liquidity and transparency. This study contributes to the literature by providing a long-horizon, dual-index analysis of weekday effects in India, linking anomalies to structural shifts and offering actionable insights for both investors and policymakers.

detail.abstract: Why anxiety, depression, and aggression are not just personal struggles, but hidden cost centers of our economies-and how a systemic model can reverse the trend. title: Tax Havens, Financial Crises, and Economic Resilience: Evidence from European Microstates
affiliations: and Beijing Normal University (BNU)

detail.title: Tax Havens, Financial Crises, and Economic Resilience: Evidence from European Microstates
detail.abstract: This article investigates the nexus between tax haven status, financial crises, and economic resilience in European microstates, focusing on Luxembourg, Liechtenstein, Monaco, and Andorra. Although microstates are often perceived as structurally vulnerable due to their small domestic markets, limited resources, and dependence on external shocks, several have shown remarkable resilience during episodes of global financial instability. Employing a mixed-methods approach, this study integrates quantitative analysis of macroeconomic indicators from 2000 to 2023 with qualitative assessment of institutional responses, policy reforms, and international negotiations. The findings demonstrate that tax haven characteristics-favorable tax regimes, financial secrecy, and niche specialization in financial services-created fiscal buffers that enhanced resilience during the 2008 global financial crisis and the COVID-19 pandemic. However, outcomes varied significantly across cases. Luxembourg's integration into European Union structures and diversified financial services enabled rapid recovery, while Liechtenstein preserved credibility through swift regulatory reforms. By contrast, Monaco and Andorra, more dependent on tourism and narrower financial systems, experienced deeper and more protracted downturns. These differences highlight that resilience is not solely a function of tax haven status but is shaped by institutional capacity, governance quality, and adaptability to shifting global norms. The study concludes that resilience in microstates is dynamic: tax haven models provide short-term advantages, but long-term stability requires diversification, regulatory compliance, and strategic reinvention. These insights contribute to broader debates on small states, global finance, and resilience theory, offering both academic and policy-oriented implications for sustaining economic stability in small, open economies.

detail.title: Energy Security, Climate Security, and National Security
detail.abstract: This article examines the complex interrelation between energy security, climate security, and national security in the contemporary geopolitical context. It contends that although climate change poses a significant security challenge, energy security remains the essential foundation of national sovereignty and systemic stability. It underscores the risks of inflexible climate policies that may jeopardize the reliability, affordability, and autonomy of energy supplies, and calls for a pragmatic, evidence-based policy approach that balances climate mitigation with the imperatives of energy infrastructure integrity and strategic stability; a nuanced, integrated framework that prioritizes energy security as central to national security.

detail.abstract: Vacancies are collapsing across advanced economies even as GDP continues to rise. In the United Kingdom, postings have fallen by more than 40% since 2022, while in the United States new evidence shows disproportionate losses among younger workers in AI-exposed occupations. This paper argues that we may be witnessing the emergence of a 'recruitment recession': a structural decoupling of growth and labor demand at the point of entry. Drawing on macro vacancy data, firm-level hiring records, and payroll evidence, we highlight the risks of narrowing on-ramps to employment and propose a research agenda to investigate the causes, mechanisms, and implications of this phenomenon. This paper calls for systematic investigation to track and analyse these dynamics at scale.

detail.abstract: The COVID-19 pandemic revealed major weaknesses in global supply chains, particularly in firms that had long depended on lean, Just-in-Time (JIT) practices. Many organizations responded by introducing Just-in-Case (JIC) buffers to improve resilience, despite the higher costs involved. This paper examines how three multinational firms-Toyota in automotive, Inditex in fast fashion, and Amazon in e-commerce-revised their inventory strategies after 2020. Using a comparative case design and secondary data from annual reports and financial databases, inventory turnover trends were tracked between 2018 and 2024. Findings show that Toyota retained its JIT discipline but added targeted safety stocks and greater supplier flexibility; Inditex adopted a hybrid model that balances rapid product cycles with readiness; and Amazon expanded fulfillment capacity and upstream inventory in line with a stronger JIC posture. This study contributes to the resilience literature by clarifying how firms recalibrate the JIT-JIC mix under systemic risk. It advances theoretical understanding by showing that resilience strategies are not dichotomous but hybrid in practice, and it offers practical insights for managers designing inventory policies under uncertainty.

detail.abstract: This chapter explores how organizational culture is created, embedded, reinforced, and transformed through deliberate and unconscious actions of leaders, structural choices, and everyday practices. detail.abstract: This paper explores the strategic integration of Six Sigma methodology with Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning (AI/ML) to drive sustainable operational excellence. Drawing from cross-industry experience-including aviation, automotive, consulting, and contact center operations-the author demonstrates how AI/ML can elevate Six Sigma from a reactive framework to a predictive engine. The paper maps AI/ML capabilities to each phase of DMAIC, offering a practical overlay that enhances speed, precision, and adaptability without compromising philosophical depth. Through real-world reflections at United Airlines, General Motors, Ford Motor Company, and contact center environments, the author illustrates how structured problem-solving and digital intelligence can work in tandem to reduce variation, improve quality, and empower the workforce. The paper emphasizes that Six Sigma is not reserved for Black Belts alone-it is a mindset accessible to anyone committed to intentional improvement. This work contributes to ongoing conversations around digital transformation, workforce equity, and legacy-building, offering a human-centered approach to operational innovation. It is intended for practitioners, strategists, and scholars seeking to bridge traditional quality frameworks with emerging technologies.

title: Innovating in Europe: Creating Value Under Constraints Overcoming Risk Inhibitors to Unlock Innovation Value

detail.abstract: Faced with accrued competition in the race to innovate and unstable geoeconomics forces, Europe competitiveness is stymied, particularly in frontier innovations. While offering significant potential returns, frontier innovations are risky, and, in the event of failure, costs are substantial, largely because of restructuring costs disproportionately high, disincentivizing European companies and resulting in a loss of competitive value. In this context, a crucial question arises: how to optimize investments in frontier innovations to turn it into a driver of competitiveness while mitigating risks? One answer is to approach innovation as a value-creation enabler, harnessing strategic opportunity gains and minimizing its costs-accounting for trade-off and hidden costs. We propose a value-driven framework to create strategic value and competitive advantage, supported by multidimensional, contextual and dynamic indicators which encompass the potential impacts of innovations within its ecosystem. As a strategic and performance management tool, a value-driven approach to innovation investment can generate shared benefits.

title: The Entrepreneurial Exodus: Political Instability, Sanctions, and the Displacement of Innovation Ecosystems -Evidence from Belarus

detail.title: The Entrepreneurial Exodus: Political Instability, Sanctions, and the Displacement of Innovation Ecosystems -Evidence from Belarus

declarations.funderStatement: This research was supported by the European Union as part of the Activity to Support Belarusian Entrepreneurship and Innovation Ecosystem. The authors thank the European Union for funding the 2023 research phase and all the entrepreneurs who shared their experiences despite personal and professional risks. Special recognition goes to the startup founders who continued building their companies while facing political persecution and sanctions challenges.

detail.abstract: This study examines the systematic displacement of entrepreneurial ecosystems under authoritarian pressure, using Belarus as a critical case study. Drawing on comprehensive longitudinal data from 220+ startups (2021) and in-depth interviews with 11 major startup founders (2023), we analyze how political instability and Western sanctions impact innovation communities. Our findings reveal a fundamental "entrepreneurial threat paradox" where authoritarian regimes simultaneously depend on and fear innovation communities. We document the largest recorded peacetime exodus of tech entrepreneurs, with 58% of Belarusian startup founders relocating internationally within one year. Paradoxically, relocated startups demonstrated enhanced performance, raising three times more capital abroad than previously. However, 64% of companies report negative impacts from sanctions, despite not being directly targeted. This research contributes to entrepreneurship literature by demonstrating how political risk shapes innovation ecosystems and provides evidence for policy frameworks supporting displaced entrepreneurial communities. Our findings have implications for understanding entrepreneurial resilience, the portability of innovation ecosystems, and the unintended consequences of economic sanctions on entrepreneurial ventures.

title: The Role of Patient Density in Improving the Effectiveness of Medicaid Managed Care
affiliations: University of Miami - Department of Management Science, Florida International University (FIU) and Florida International University (FIU) - College of Business

detail.title: The Role of Patient Density in Improving the Effectiveness of Medicaid Managed Care
detail.abstract: Medicaid Managed Care (MMC) has become the dominant delivery model for low-income populations in the United States, yet its effectiveness varies widely across hospitals. This study examines how the density of MMC patients within a hospital's caseload influences its response to capitation-based incentives. We introduce the concept of density-driven operational adaptation, which posits that a higher concentration of MMC patients increases the salience of payer incentives and motivates hospitals to realign workflows, discharge planning, and post-acute coordination. Using a natural experiment created by Florida's transition from fee-for-service to statewide MMC between 2013 and 2015, we find that hospitals with higher MMC density achieve shorter inpatient stays, higher post-acute care utilization, and lower 30-day readmissions and emergency department visits. These improvements are concentrated in postoperative care, where coordination and discharge timing are most critical, and are driven by current patient mix rather than accumulated experience. Our findings highlight the critical role of patient-type density in shaping the success of value-based payment reforms, with implications for policymakers seeking to strengthen MMC effectiveness and for hospital managers aiming to align operations with payer-driven incentives.

Through his contrasting experience with another new employee, the case provides insight into workplace culture, favouritism, and the impact of exclusion on employee motivation. The study serves as an example for discussions on organizational behaviour, human resource practices, and employee engagement.

detail.abstract: We provide evidence that bank loan supply reactions to monetary policy changes are market-specific, emphasizing the importance of banks’ local specialization. We analyze the U.S. mortgage market and find that when monetary policy eases, banks increase new mortgage lending growth more in markets in which they are geographically specialized relative to other markets and banks. This holds after controlling for local lending opportunities and (unobservable) bank differences. Further empirical findings, supported by a simple model, suggest that banks face market-specific differences in lending advantages, related to market-specific information, leading them to exhibit different reactions to monetary policy changes. We document the aggregate effects of this geographical specialization channel both at the county (regional) level on mortgage supply and house price growth, as well as at the bank level on average specialization growth. Our study underscores the relevance of banks’ local specialization in shaping the transmission of monetary policy.

title: Service Quality in Southeast Asian Tourism: Comparative Insights from Vietnam and Thailand

detail.title: Service Quality in Southeast Asian Tourism: Comparative Insights from Vietnam and Thailand
detail.abstract:
This study investigates the service quality of the tourism industry in Southeast Asia, focusing on a comparative analysis between Vietnam and Thailand. Using online customer reviews as the primary dataset, we applied text mining and sentiment analysis techniques based on the SERVQUAL framework to assess five service quality dimensions: tangibles, reliability, responsiveness, assurance, and empathy.

The findings reveal that Vietnam demonstrates a higher proportion of positive reviews (27.5%) compared to Thailand (23.7%), with notably lower negative sentiment. Vietnam outperforms Thailand particularly in the dimensions of tangibles and assurance, suggesting that improvements in facilities, accommodation standards, and staff professionalism have contributed to enhanced visitor satisfaction.

These results highlight Vietnam’s growing competitiveness in the post-pandemic tourism recovery period and provide practical implications for policymakers and industry stakeholders seeking to strengthen service quality as a driver of sustainable growth in the regional tourism sector.

detail.abstract: This paper explores motivational challenges among Construction and Infrastructure Technical Officers in Sri Lanka's construction and civil engineering sectors through the lens of Vroom's Expectancy Theory (Vroom, 1964). Construction and Infrastructure Technical Officers, including those in road construction, water projects, building projects, and other infrastructure works, often perform under challenging conditions such as long-distance travel, difficult site visits, and responsibilities beyond their formal roles, including site supervision, technical work, and liaison between stakeholders. Despite their contributions, many face low salaries, minimal recognition, limited benefits, and public criticism for project delays or errors, weakening the link between effort, performance, and valued rewards. The content reflects the author's interpretation of informal discussions with a selection of Construction and Infrastructure Technical Officers and may not represent all officers' experiences. The primary purpose of this study is to raise awareness of these motivational issues and to encourage further, wider-ranging studies to determine the prevalence of dissatisfaction, underlying causes, and potential solutions within the sector.

title: Developing a Comprehensive Psychometric Tool to Measure Multidimensional Quotients: An Integrative Approach to IQ, EQ, SQ, and FQ
affiliations: Independent and SVKM'S NMIMS Hyderabad

detail.title: Developing a Comprehensive Psychometric Tool to Measure Multidimensional Quotients: An Integrative Approach to IQ, EQ, SQ, and FQ
detail.abstract: In the 21st century, success and resilience demand more than traditional measures of intelligence. While IQ (Intelligence Quotient) dominates as a benchmark for historical cognitive capacity, research highlights the increasing importance of other domains-Emotional Quotient (EQ), Social Quotient (SQ), and Financial Quotient (FQ)-that determine overall human functioning. This paper introduces a novel psychometric tool (MQS), a tool designed to assess individuals in these four dimensions. Drawing from the principles of neuropsychology and neurocognitive training, MQS gives intelligence information not only as a static feature, but also as an adaptive resource, which is influenced by cognitive processes and socioemotional learning. Each domain is severely reviewed: as IQ cognitive logic, EQ as emotional regulation and sympathy, SQ as mutual adaptability, and FQ as financial literacy and decision making. The purpose of the scale is to integrate these interconnected constructions into a single piece and fill an existing difference in evaluation devices. Literature reviews show that high integration of these quotes promotes flexibility, adaptability and better decision-making in students and professionals. Practical implications include its use to promote well-rounded, flexible individuals in educational institutions, workplaces and medical intervention. MQS has been deployed as an essential clinical and developmental instrument to enhance life skills, prepare students for real-world challenges and help grow into an uncertain socioeconomic environment.

title: The Enduring Blueprint: Biblical Leadership and Its Timeless Lessons on Power, Purpose, and Principle
affiliations: City University of New York (CUNY) - Koppelman School of Business and CUNY Brooklyn College

detail.title: The Enduring Blueprint: Biblical Leadership and Its Timeless Lessons on Power, Purpose, and Principle
detail.abstract: In a brittle, anxious, non-linear, and incomprehensible (BANI) world, traditional leadership is failing. With 80% of people expecting organizations to help solve major societal issues, a new approach is urgently needed. This paper argues that purpose-driven leadership, rooted in ancient Hebrew biblical narratives, offers a powerful and timeless framework. We examine how biblical principles of justice (mishpat), righteousness (tzedaka), and lovingkindness (chesed) serve as a model for authentic leadership. By examining figures like Abraham, Moses, and David, the study demonstrates how effective leadership is a purpose-driven calling grounded in transcendent values, not merely a service. These leaders exemplified accountability and a profound commitment to the vulnerable, providing practical guidance for navigating today's complex ethical challenges. Ultimately, the paper concludes that purpose-driven leadership, informed by this ancient wisdom, is both a moral imperative and a strategic necessity for building resilience and fostering flourishing in our interconnected world.

title: The Future of Smart Warehousing: Scope of Integrated AI-Powered Real-Time Data Tracking and Robotics for Optimizing Complex Operations

detail.title: The Future of Smart Warehousing: Scope of Integrated AI-Powered Real-Time Data Tracking and Robotics for Optimizing Complex Operations
detail.abstract: Supply chain management (SCM) is being revolutionized by smart warehousing, which combines modern technologies, equipment's, robotics and artificial intelligence (AI). Processing orders delays, excessive expenses and bottlenecks challenge traditional warehousing procedures. Realtime jobs which are driven by AI, augments decision-making process with real-time data monitoring, automates stock replenishment and improves forecasting. By integrating automating material handling, picking and packaging, robotics will further simplify the processes while minimizing the possibilities of errors and operating expenses. This study examines how robotics and artificial intelligence might work together to maximize warehouse productivity. Predictive analytics, automated robotic process automation (RPA) and machine learning for demand forecasting hold due importance in development. But there are still a lot of obstacles to overcome, like high implementation costs, cybersecurity issues and worker's ability to adapt.

title: Invisible Governance: Trust Protocols for AI-Driven Franchise Ecosystems
affiliations: Hoopoe Holding Ltd.

detail.title: Invisible Governance: Trust Protocols for AI-Driven Franchise Ecosystems
detail.abstract: Franchising has long relied on visible enforcement, contracts, manuals, audits, inspections, to hold networks together. As systems globalize, integrate AI, and navigate regulatory fragmentation, this scaffolding proves slow, brittle, and expensive. A more durable architecture is emerging: invisible governance. In this model, trust is not imposed externally but designed directly into the structure of the network. This paper develops invisible governance as a continuation of my earlier argument that franchises must be understood as intelligent organisms. If networks are alive, their survival depends not on external policing but on circulatory mechanisms of trust. I propose a three-pillar framework: explainable algorithmic systems; blockchain-anchored compliance through self-executing contracts; and organizational philosophy embedded as cultural DNA. Drawing on 15 years of polyclinic franchise experience in the GCC, recent system design at Hoopoe Holding, and comparative evidence from health and beauty ecosystems worldwide, the study shows how invisible governance reduces disputes, lowers transaction costs, and reassures investors. The conclusion is direct: in the franchise systems of the future, trust will not be supervised; it will be engineered into the very DNA of the network.

detail.abstract: Pharmacies have long been a lucrative revenue source for retailers, yet their role as traffic drivers and their broader impact on cross-category revenue remain understudied. This paper quantifies the spillover effects of pharmacy improvements using quasiexperimental variation from a national chain's in-store pharmacy re-branding. Using a series of difference-indifferences analyses, I estimate that the rebranding led to an 8.5% increase in visits to non-pharmacy categories and a 9.6% rise in non-pharmacy spending. Further analyses suggest that the cross-category spillover is driven by consumers seeking the convenience of one-stop shopping. However, the effect weakens when consumers face higher switching costs in transitioning to a new pharmacy provider. These findings provide strategic insights for retailers, underscoring the need to minimize the switching hassle when improving pharmacies for higher cross-category demand.

detail.abstract: By personalization, predictive analytics, and recommendation systems, artificial intelligence (AI) is changing consumer behavior, particularly post-purchase behavior. To understand the multifaceted impact of AI on consumer behavior, this study examines how AI-driven technologies like recommendation systems and personalization tools influence post-purchase behaviors. We uncover key outcomes, such as satisfaction, loyalty, and dissatisfaction, through the integration of empirical research and theoretical frameworks. Although AI enhances consumer experiences through tailored recommendations and predictive insights, it also raises ethical concerns regarding data privacy, algorithmic bias, and data security. To increase consumer satisfaction and loyalty, AI systems not only personalize content but also predict and adapt to evolving preferences. However, these technologies often operate without consumers' full awareness, making it challenging to distinguish between beneficial personalization and manipulative design. The study encourages the adoption of responsible AI practices. We conclude by suggesting future studies direction that emphasize long-term effects and applications across diverse sectors.

title: Incentives, Burnout, and Turnover: Dynamic Compensation Design with Effort Cost Spillover

detail.title: Incentives, Burnout, and Turnover: Dynamic Compensation Design with Effort Cost Spillover

contentType.other: This is the preprint version of a paper that has been accepted but not yet published.

detail.abstract: Employee burnout has long plagued firms. The prevalence of burnout shows that work-related effort is not only costly in the present but has carryover effects into the future. We incorporate this 'effort cost spillover' into a dynamic, twoperiod principal-agent model, where the worker's effort cost in the second period increases in both their second-period and first-period efforts. We use this model to explore optimal compensation design and the connection between incentives, burnout, and turnover. Naturally, turnover may occur if it is easy to replace workers, or if firms fail to account for burnout when designing contracts. However, we show that even when turnover is very costly, and firms and workers properly understand effort cost spillover, the firm's equilibrium strategy may be to offer high-powered incentives that induce workers to work so hard that they exit (i.e. reject any contract that the firm would offer) in the next period. Workplace measures that reduce spillover, such as flexible work arrangements, can limit turnover and improve profits dramatically. Committing to contracts for both periods in advance can also limit turnover (at the cost of reduced flexibility).

detail.title: The Influence of Employee Health and Safety Policies on the Value of the Firm
detail.abstract: This study investigates the impact of Health and Safety (H&S) policies on the valuation of over 2,000 United States firms, where results indicate the existence of a significant positive value elevation as a result of successful H&S Employee Policies implementation, with evidence of moderate variation partly attributed to the influence of the Patient Protection and Affordable Care Act (ACA). Crucially, the study establishes that the observed impact of H&S policies on firm value is not a result of an implicit reaction to policy implementation due to the COVID-19 pandemic, but a consistent trend over a prolonged period, underscoring the strategic importance of H&S policies in corporate valuation. The study presents a series of tests that demonstrate the particular benefit of H&S Policy in enhancing the value of firms.

title: Strategy as Ontology: From Metaphor to Mechanism in Strategic Thought - QCEA-P and QCEA-T Formalised Mathematically
affiliations: Rhodes University

detail.title: Strategy as Ontology: From Metaphor to Mechanism in Strategic Thought - QCEA-P and QCEA-T Formalised Mathematically
detail.abstract: This article introduces the Quantum-Complex-Entropic-Adaptive Paradigm (QCEA-P) and its accompanying Quantum-Complex-Entropic-Adaptive Theory (QCEA-T) as a unified, falsifiable foundation for strategic thought. QCEA-P defines the high-level framework: genuine strategy arises only when four conditions are satisfied-irreducible uncertainty, a closed information-action cycle, nonzero organisational coherence, and recursive quantum-open-system dynamics. QCEA-T supplies the formal machinery: modelling strategic states as density operators on a finite Hilbert space and decisions as POVM measurements, it derives eighteen Strategic Laws-formal invariants each accompanied by a mathematical formulation, an empirical test protocol, a characteristic signature, and a real-world example. In the limit of commuting observables and vanishing entropy, classical planning and game theory re-emerge as special cases of QCEA-T (Theorem A.1). An empirical programme links state-tomography methods (Eq. A.25) and sample-size formulas (Eq. A.22) to practitioner metrics, enabling early-warning diagnostics and spectral-gap design. Implications for management practice include monitoring coherence functionals, timing interventions near critical couplings, and employing order-effect diagnostics as leading indicators of strategic drift. By moving "from metaphor to mechanism," the QCEA-P/T framework elevates strategy into a mature, cross-disciplinary science with cumulative theory and falsifiable constructs.

title: Quantum Machine Learning for Cost Variance Analysis in Industrial Manufacturing Processes: A Computational Breakthrough
affiliations: Arkansas State University

detail.title: Quantum Machine Learning for Cost Variance Analysis in Industrial Manufacturing Processes: A Computational Breakthrough
detail.abstract: This study presents a quantum machine learning framework for improving cost variance analysis in industrial manufacturing. It addresses the challenges posed by classical methods when handling highdimensional and nonlinear industrial process cost data. By integrating Quantum Support Vector Machines (QSVMs) with quantum kernel methods, the framework uses quantum-enhanced feature mapping to transform cost data into a high-dimensional Hilbert space where complex patterns become more separable. A rigorous numerical experiment is conducted using a synthetic dataset that simulates real-world manufacturing cost variations, including price, efficiency, and volume variances. The results indicate that while a classical SVM with a radial basis function kernel failed to detect anomalies, the QSVM achieved a precision of 21%, a recall of 40%, and an F1 score of 27%, along with a shorter training time. These findings validate the hypothesis that quantum approaches can effectively capture nonlinear interdependencies among cost drivers and improve anomaly detection. Despite promising performance, the study acknowledges current limitations in quantum hardware scalability and interpretability. Overall, this work not only advances the theoretical understanding of quantum machine learning for cost analysis but also lays the groundwork for future practical implementations in process optimization and decision support within complex industrial environments.

title: When Supply Lowers Demand: Evidence from an Invitation-Only Policy Reform in Digital Asset Marketplaces

detail.title: When Supply Lowers Demand: Evidence from an Invitation-Only Policy Reform in Digital Asset Marketplaces
detail.abstract: Digital asset marketplaces, such as NFT marketplaces, merge primary and secondary markets, enabling resales. While resale royalties in such resale-centric settings are well studied, the impact of expanding primary supply is less understood. Cross-side network theory predicts that more supply should raise demand; however, a substitution effect may emerge. When primary supply competes with secondary listings, greater primary supply can reduce secondary resale opportunities and thereby dampen demand. We study this mechanism using Foundation's removal of invitation-only onboarding on May 19, 2022, with SuperRare as a comparison market. Using a difference-indifferences design, we find that Foundation experiences a 1.9% average weekly decline in bids, 8.8% among active traders, consistent with the substitution effect. Traders with greater resale experience bid less, suggesting heightened uncertainty about resale profits. When prior resales are successful, traders are more willing to bid on riskier NFTs from new minters or those with potential copyright concerns. On the supply side, minters reduce listings by 7.5%, with larger declines among those who had invitation privileges. Our results inform supply controls of resale-focused marketplaces.

title: Artificial Intelligence and Employee Satisfaction
affiliations: , Shanghai Jiao Tong University (SJTU) - Antai College of Economics and Management, Shanghai Jiao Tong University - Antai College of Economics and Management and University of Washington - Michael G. Foster School of Business

detail.title: Artificial Intelligence and Employee Satisfaction
detail.abstract: The integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in the workplace has transformed organizational dynamics, raising important questions about how AI reshapes employee well-being. To address this, we introduce a novel, task-level measure of occupational AI exposure, developed using advanced NLP techniques and calculated by integrating 6.17 million Glassdoor employee ratings (2008-2023), O*NET occupational characteristics, and Google Patents Public data to quantify the extent to which job tasks are affected by AI technologies across firms and over time. Using a general equilibrium framework, our model shows that AI exposure increases employee utility by raising equilibrium wages and reducing working hours, which together contribute to greater employee satisfaction. To empirically test these predictions, we examine the relationship between occupational AI exposure and employee satisfaction, finding a significant positive association even after controlling for software and robotics adoption. Further, leveraging ChatGPT-based task decomposition, we find that these gains are primarily driven by AI augmentation-boosting both compensation and work-life balance. These findings are robust to specifications using individual-level IPUMS U.S. Census and American Community Survey microdata, where we observe heterogeneous effects by age, education, race, gender, and income. Taken together, our theoretical and empirical results suggest that, rather than merely disrupting workplaces, the chaos of AI-driven change can serve as a ladder-enabling strategic adoption that enhances both the economic and overall well-being of employees in the modern workplace.

detail.abstract: Background: In this study, the parameters that directly impact purchase intentions were analysed, such as electronic word of mouth, customer engagement, brand awareness, and customer retention. Objectives: This study aimed to explore the impact of digital content marketing on customer purchase intentions. Methods/Approach: The study used Partial Least Square Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM) to explore the hypothesised relationships between variables and the extent to which digital content marketing strategies influence purchase intention. Results: The study's findings highlighted that content marketing positively impacts electronic word of mouth, brand awareness, customer retention, and customer engagement. In contrast, the results revealed that content marketing does not directly impact purchase intentions. Conclusions: The study's results indicate that digital content marketing affects purchase intentions indirectly, primarily through customer engagement, brand awareness, customer retention, and electronic word of mouth. In essence, the complete impact of digital content marketing on purchase intention is realised through these indirect factors. The findings enrich the literature on digital content marketing and provide some practical implications for companies to invest more in this direction to improve their performance.

title: Dark Patterns as Disloyal Design
affiliations: Northeastern University Khoury College of Computer Sciences, Boston University School of Law, Washington University School of Law, Northeastern University Khoury College of Computer Sciences and Northeastern University

detail.title: Dark Patterns as Disloyal Design
detail.abstract:
Lawmakers have started to regulate “dark patterns,” understood to be design practices meant to influence technology users’ decisions through manipulative or deceptive means. Most agree that dark patterns are undesirable, but open questions remain as to which design choices should be subjected to scrutiny, much less the best way to regulate them.

In this Article, we propose adapting the concept of dark patterns to better fit legal frameworks. Critics allege that the legal conceptualizations of dark patterns are overbroad, impractical, and counterproductive. We argue that law and policy conceptualizations of dark patterns suffer from three deficiencies: First, dark patterns lack a clear value anchor for cases to build upon. Second, legal definitions of dark patterns overfocus on individuals and atomistic choices, ignoring de minimis aggregate harms and the societal implications of manipulation at scale. Finally, the law has struggled to articulate workable legal thresholds for wrongful dark patterns. To better regulate the designs called dark patterns, lawmakers need a better conceptual framing that bridges the gap between design theory and the law’s need for clarity, flexibility, and compatibility with existing frameworks.

We argue that wrongful self-dealing is at the heart of what most consider to be “dark” about certain design patterns. Taking advantage of design affordances to the detriment of a vulnerable party is disloyal. To that end, we propose disloyal design is a regulatory framing for dark patterns. In drawing from established frameworks that prohibit wrongful self-dealing, we hope to provide more clarity and consistency for regulators, industry, and users. Disloyal design will fit better into legal frameworks and better rally public support for ensuring that the most popular tools in society are built to prioritize human values.

detail.abstract: Headline figures such as “80–95% of AI projects fail” have shaped executive perceptions of enterprise AI. This working paper conducts a targeted scoping review of recent gray‑literature reports and commentary: RAND (2024), MIT/Project NANDA (2025). Section’s AI Proficiency (2025), Gartner commentary (2019), press analyses, and a podcast episode, to assess what the data actually support. We find consistent directional evidence of a pilot‑to‑production gap and organizational constraints (problem framing, data readiness, change management, sponsorship, integration) outweighing technical limitations. None of the sources employs probability sampling or standardized outcome definitions suitable for population‑level prevalence claims; thus, headline failure rates should be treated as hypothesis‑generating rather than inferential. We synthesize implications for leadership and propose a real‑options approach to funding AI portfolios to mitigate downside while preserving upside.

title: Quantity or Quality of Children? Fertility, Human Capital, and Inheritance of Tastes for Education Investment
affiliations: Central South University and

detail.title: Quantity or Quality of Children? Fertility, Human Capital, and Inheritance of Tastes for Education Investment
detail.abstract: East Asia is characterized by notably low fertility rates and high private education investment. This phenomenon is frequently attributed to the cultural emphasis on education, often referred to as "education fever". This paper introduces a new theoretical mechanism that links high private education spending to low fertility rates. It proposes that parents' decisions on education investment are influenced by intergenerationally transmitted tastes, where the extent of education investments they experienced shapes their spendings for their children. Utilizing an overlapping generations model, this paper examines both the short-and long-term effects of these education tastes on fertility and economic outcomes. The findings reveal three main insights: (1) strong preference for inherited tastes for education investment leads to a high growth rate of human capital, a high capital stock, but a low fertility rate both in the intertemporal equilibria and the steady states; (2) under strong preference for the taste, the growth rate of human capital and the capital stock increase, while the fertility rate decreases along the transition path; (3) there may exist turning periods, after which the speed of convergence changes from acceleration to deceleration. These insights provide both theoretical and policy implications pertinent to addressing the challenges associated with declining fertility rates and high education spendings across East Asia.

title: Exploring Influencing Factors to Incorporation by Reference Use: A Comparative Analysis of Canada and the United States

detail.title: Exploring Influencing Factors to Incorporation by Reference Use: A Comparative Analysis of Canada and the United States
detail.abstract: There is a long literature on standards, regulation, and legislation as forms of regulatory governance. Yet, little research has explored the combination of these forms of regulatory governance and what factors influence these combinations' use. One such combination is incorporation by reference (IbR)-where a particular standard becomes referenced within a regulation or legislation. While we know IbR has been widely used in the United States (US) and Canada, it is unclear what the influencing factors are to these IbR uses. Past regulatory governance research has found that regulatory and legislative, government-wide and department/agency-level policy, and international body policy efforts can influence particular forms of regulatory governance usage. This paper explores these previously identified influencing factors against IbR use across Canada and the US. This exploration was completed using a novel dataset of Canadian IbR instances (1400+ instances from 1946 to 2024) and an existing dataset of the US's IbR instances (26000+ instances from 1931 to 2024). Our findings suggest that Canadian regulatory and legislative IbR efforts have more influence over IbR usage than the other influencing factors. While the US shows mixed results across these influencing factors, with some seemingly leading to increases in IbR usage and others being followed by decreases or unchanged usage trends. We also found that Canada took a concerted approach, with almost all influence efforts being taken over a short duration, while the US's influencing efforts took place over several decades. The pervasive use of IbR demands further scholarly attention given its consequences for regulatory governance, such as the trade-offs between expertise and efficiency and giving private actors power to shape regulatory provisions; concerted vs. fragmented policy efforts around regulatory governance; and government decision-making around IbR national or international standards, and the implications of those decisions.

title: Permanent Capital Losses after Banking Crises
affiliations: Georgetown University, European Central Bank (ECB), University of Luxembourg and Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) - Sloan School of Management

detail.title: Permanent Capital Losses after Banking Crises

publicationDetails.journalName: NBER Working Paper Series

detail.abstract:
We study the mechanisms driving bank losses across historical banking crises in 46 economies and the effectiveness of policy interventions in restoring bank capitalization. We find that bank stocks experience large, permanent declines at the onset of crises. These losses predict commensurate long-term declines in banks’ earnings and dividends, rather than elevated future equity returns. Bank losses are primarily driven by write-downs of nonperforming assets, not asset sales during panics. Forceful liquidity-based interventions during crises predict only small, temporary increases in bank market value. Overall, these results suggest that bank losses during crises are not primarily due to temporary price dislocations. Early liquidity interventions can avert banking crises, but only under specific conditions. Once large bank equity declines have occurred, policy responses have historically failed to prevent persistent undercapitalization in the banking sector.

publicationDetails.journalName: NBER Working Paper Series

detail.abstract:
We study the optimal allocation of population and consumption in a dynamic spatial general equilibrium model with frictional migration, where households' idiosyncratic location preference shocks are private information. We derive a recursive formula for the constrained-efficient allocation, capturing the trade-off between consumption smoothing and efficient migration. In a quantitative model calibrated to the US economy featuring both cross-state migration and risk-free savings, we find that the constrained-efficient allocation features lower population but higher average consumption in less productive states than the status quo, achieving efficiency and spatial redistribution simultaneously through dynamic incentives. In response to local negative productivity shocks, the constrained-efficient allocation features more front-loaded consumption than the status quo, with systematic heterogeneity linked to the location’s pre-shock fundamentals.

title: Small States in Europe and Global Shocks: Divergent Paths of Growth and Convergence, 2000-2023

detail.title: Small States in Europe and Global Shocks: Divergent Paths of Growth and Convergence, 2000-2023
detail.abstract: This article examines the economic trajectories of small European states from 2000 to 2023 in the context of successive global shocks. Despite structural vulnerabilities-such as limited market size, high trade dependence, and constrained fiscal autonomy-many small states have demonstrated notable resilience and adaptability. The period under review encompasses major disruptions: the dot-com downturn, the 2008-2009 global financial crisis, the Eurozone debt crisis, the refugee and migration challenges of the 2010s, Brexit, the COVID-19 pandemic, and the geopolitical and energy shocks following Russia's 2022 invasion of Ukraine. Drawing on comparative analysis, the article highlights the divergence in growth and convergence paths among small states, which include both high-income Western European countries (e.g., Ireland, Luxembourg, Denmark, Finland) and post-transition economies in Central and Eastern Europe (e.g., Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania, Slovenia, Slovakia). While some states leveraged institutional simplicity, digital infrastructure, and export-oriented strategies to recover swiftly, others suffered prolonged downturns due to financial fragility or reliance on vulnerable sectors like tourism. The study identifies three overarching dynamics: (1) global shocks consistently magnified structural constraints; (2) EU integration served as both a buffer and a constraint; and (3) domestic policy agility and strategic positioning within global value chains determined resilience. Ultimately, the article contributes to a more nuanced understanding of small states as neither uniformly fragile nor uniformly successful, but as diverse actors whose responses to global shocks are shaped by the interplay of external pressures and internal capacities.

title: A Nascent International Financial Channel of China’s Monetary Policy Transmission

detail.abstract:
Chinese private portfolio equity outflows, though small compared to other Chinese outflows, are growing rapidly because of capital account liberalization and capital flight. Using granular stock-holding data on Qualified Domestic Institutional Investor (QDII) mutual funds, we identify a nascent financial channel of international transmission of Chinese monetary policy to world stocks. Event study analysis around monetary policy announcement days reveals that monetary policy tightening depresses returns of country equity indexes and individual U.S. stocks with QDII fund exposure relative to non-exposed stocks. The results are robust to controlling for the real transmission channel of Chinese monetary policy and other confounders. The effect is driven by smaller and less liquid firms, but not by China-concept stocks or those highly exposed to China's macroeconomic shocks. We also find that the results are driven by household portfolio rebalancing from more to less risky assets following the announcement.

detail.abstract: We suggest a core set of indicators for evaluating the position of the labor market relative to maximum employment.  The unemployment rate remains the key indicator of the cyclical position of the labor market, as it is time-tested, is highly correlated with other indicators, and has practical measurement advantages. But other indicators can provide complementary evidence to get a fuller picture of the labor market.  A joint analysis of job vacancies and unemployment in a Beveridge curve diagram is helpful when structural shocks affect the labor market and when the labor market is very tight, while the employment-to-population ratio is useful late in expansions, when increases in employment tend to arise from higher labor force participation.  Additional indicators—including wage growth and worker flows—can complement the core indicators we discuss.  We draw on lessons from the Global Financial Crisis and the COVID-19 pandemic to evaluate the effectiveness of various indicators.

detail.title: Identity as Self-Image

detail.abstract:
We review the economic literature on self-image, which conceptualizes identity as a set of beliefs about one’s core traits, values, goals, and social ties. Self-image concerns lead individuals to process information and make choices in non-standard ways that help affirm and protect certain valued identities. We first present the main cognitive mechanisms involved within a simple unifying framework. We then survey the extensive laboratory, online, and field experimental literature on the nature and behavioral implications of self-image concerns. We discuss in particular how they give rise to information and decision avoidance, motivated memory and beliefs, excuse-driven behavior, preferences for truth-telling, hypothetical bias, moral cleansing and moral licensing, collective identities, political preferences, and other forms of self-signaling or self-deception. We subsequently discuss common empirical strategies used to identify self-image concerns, as well as the threats to their validity and how to alleviate them. We conclude by outlining open questions and directions for future research on the belief-based approach to identity.

This paper proposes a non-pecuniary measure of career achievement, seniority. Based on a database of over 150 million resumes, this metric exploits the variation in how long it takes workers to attain job titles. A person’s seniority is defined as the number of years it takes the median individual—within the same industry and firm size category—to achieve that person’s job title. Seniority aligns with standard markers of success—it is positively correlated with both wages and educational attainment. To demonstrate its value as a measure of career progression, we show that individuals with higher seniority levels in the public sector are more likely to transition to higher-paying positions in the private sector. When non-monetary factors influence career choice, evaluating labor market outcomes using non-wage measures, such as seniority, offers significant advantages.

title: The Traffic Noise Externality: Costs, Incidence and Policy Implications
affiliations: University of California, Berkeley - Department of Economics and University of Toronto

detail.title: The Traffic Noise Externality: Costs, Incidence and Policy Implications

publicationDetails.journalName: NBER Working Paper Series

detail.abstract:
More than 42 million Americans are exposed to medium or high levels of traffic noise. Despite its potentially large toll and unequal distribution, the economic costs, incidence, and policy implications of traffic noise have received limited attention in economics. We quantify the aggregate economic burden of this externality and its distribution across demographic groups by estimating homebuyers' willingness to pay for quieter environments. Using quasi-experimental variation from the construction of noise barriers, we find that reduced traffic noise exposure leads to significant increases in house prices, implying that buyers are willing to pay a substantial premium for each decibel of noise reduction. In the five years before construction, we detect no differential pre-trends in prices between treated and control properties. Following construction, we observe an immediate and largely permanent 6.8% increase in prices within 100 meters, with smaller gains at greater distances. Information on each barrier's noise attenuation allows us to recover the willingness to pay per decibel of traffic noise. We calculate the aggregate economic cost of traffic noise at $110 billion nationwide. The economic burden is disproportionately borne by lower income and minority households, suggesting that the externality is regressive. The cost varies widely across cities, reflecting differences in noise levels, property values and population density. Based on our estimates, the socially efficient Pigouvian tax amounts to $974 per vehicle. A broad shift to electric vehicles -- which are quieter than traditional vehicles -- could yield noise reduction benefits of $77.3 billion, concentrated among low-income families in dense urban areas.

We study the large-scale implementation of a system of specialized domestic violence courts (SDVCs), an innovation in access to justice programs for potential victims of intimate partner violence (IPV) and offenders. Access to SDVCs leads to a considerable 8 percentage points increase in the probability that judges issue a protection order and a 1.7 percentage point (15 percent) decrease in victim and offender reappearance rates within one year of the start of the case. Effects are more pronounced for cases in which parties have children in common and in which access to SDVCs is more limited. Linking the case data to administrative and survey data on judges, we show that the priorities of judges assigned to SDVCs play a prominent role in explaining these outcomes.
